# Conway's Original 1968 Thesis

According to the page, Conway's original thesis statement is:

"Any organization that designs a system (defined broadly) will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure."

This formulation appeared in his 1968 Datamation publication after the Harvard Business Review rejected the paper two years earlier.

# The Microservice Premium

**Core Claim:**

Martin Fowler argues that microservices impose significant costs that only make sense beyond a certain complexity threshold. He states: "When you use microservices you have to work on automated deployment, monitoring, dealing with failure, eventual consistency, and other factors" (121 characters).

**The Key Threshold:**

The decisive factor is system complexity. Fowler's central recommendation: "don't even consider microservices unless you have a system that's too complex to manage as a monolith" (97 characters).

**What Justifies the Premium:**

Fowler identifies sources of complexity that warrant microservices adoption—large teams, multi-tenancy, diverse user interaction models, independent business function evolution, and scaling demands. However, he emphasizes that "the biggest factor is that of sheer size - people finding they have a monolith that's too big to modify and deploy."

**The Bottom Line:**

Without sufficient complexity to warrant the overhead, microservices become a liability rather than a solution. Fowler cautions that "the microservices approach brings a high premium, one that can slow down your development considerably."

# Fowler on Team Size, Operational Complexity, and Monoliths

**On team size and modularity:**
"Good modular structure is useful in any program, but becomes exponentially more important as the software grows in size. Perhaps more importantly, it grows more in importance as the team developing it grows in size."

**On operational complexity:**
Fowler emphasizes that microservices create significant operational overhead: "half-a-dozen applications now turn into hundreds of little microservices" requiring continuous deployment capabilities and DevOps culture—skills that become mandatory rather than merely beneficial.

**On when monoliths are preferable:**
Fowler states the key principle directly: "there is a Microservice Premium: microservices impose a cost on productivity that can only be made up for in more complex systems. So if you can manage your system's complexity with a monolithic architecture then you shouldn't be using microservices."

**Note on specific thresholds:**
The article provides no explicit numerical thresholds (like "teams over X people" or "systems with Y services"). The guidance remains contextual rather than prescriptive, emphasizing that architectural choices depend on your specific situation's complexity level.

182	## Verdict Block Format
183	
184	The six verdict blocks are emitted together under the single top-level heading
185	`## Self-Audit Gate (process output)`, one `##` heading holding all six in criterion order —
186	the same placement the adversarial pass record and the self-audit scan prescribe for themselves.
187	They are one artifact, not six; nesting them beneath another section's heading makes them a
188	subsection of something they do not belong to, and a reader or a check keyed to that heading
189	must find it in the same structural position on every run.
190	
191	Each of the 6 criteria requires exactly one verdict block. Use the standard form when the
192	analysis section exists and contains scoreable content:
193	
194	```text
195	**Criterion N: [Criterion Name]**
196	Quoted span: "[Direct quote of the specific text that most directly determines the band assigned — from the analysis being scored, or, per the admission below, from the self-audit scan for Criteria 4 and 6 or the Assumption Audit scan for Criterion 2, each emitted as process output for this analysis.]"
197	Band: [**Rigorous** / **Sound** / **Hand-wavy** / **Absent**]
198	Justification: [One sentence tying the quoted span to the observable descriptor for
199	that band — name the specific structural property present or absent.]
200	```
201	
202	The self-audit scan and the Assumption Audit scan are not output sections, and they are the only artifacts outside the six-section analysis a verdict block may quote: the self-audit scan for Criteria 4 and 6, and the Assumption Audit scan for Criterion 2. Every other criterion quotes the analysis text itself, and the §6→§4 closure ledger is admitted nowhere — it is a drafting artifact that describes a document other than the one being scored.
203	
204	Use the gap-citation form when the criterion scores Absent because the section or named
205	artifact is missing or empty — in that case there is no span to quote, and the documented
206	absence is the evidence:
207	
208	```text
209	**Criterion N: [Criterion Name]**
210	Gap: [Name what is missing and where it should have appeared — e.g., "No Derivation
211	Chains section exists; chains of the form 'GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate] → [conclusion]'
212	should appear in section 4 (Derivation Chains) for each conclusion stated in section 6
213	(Conclusion)."]
214	Band: Absent
215	Justification: [One sentence: the absence itself is the structural failure that triggers
216	the gate — the criterion cannot be scored against a non-existent artifact.]
217	```
218	
219	Verdict blocks (not a consolidated table) are required because each block contains a quoted
220	span or a gap citation. Without that span, the evidence-quoting requirement cannot be audited:
221	a summary table of band labels can be produced by asserting compliance, but a verdict block
222	containing a quote that contradicts its claimed band creates a contradiction that cannot be
223	sustained.

234	### Criterion 1: Identify Essence
235	
236	Scores the **Essence Statement** — the single sentence naming the core problem followed by
237	a short list of success criteria — in the Problem Essence section (output section 1).
238	
239	- **Rigorous** — the Essence Statement is a single sentence that names the core question or
240	  decision (not a symptom, not the triggering event, not a restatement of the user's prompt);
241	  each success criterion contains a pass/fail structural test — a verb + subject + outcome
242	  triplet where the outcome is a property of the Conclusion section — so that a reviewer
243	  applies each criterion by scanning the Conclusion section without analyst interpretation;
244	  the statement is specific enough that it appears nowhere in an analysis of a different but
245	  related problem without modification (it names a property unique to this problem, not a
246	  generic template phrase).
247	  If this section uses the honest-depth escape valve (`Nothing material here — [reason]`), the
248	  stated reason is specific to this analysis's problem — it names a property of the problem
249	  that makes an Essence Statement unnecessary or redundant, and that reason appears in no
250	  other analysis without alteration.
251	
252	- **Sound** — the Essence Statement exists and names a question, but the success criteria are
253	  vague or stated in terms that cannot be verified against the conclusion without further
254	  clarification (e.g., "the solution should be good," "the approach should be appropriate").
255	
256	- **Hand-wavy** — the Essence Statement exists but names a symptom, a triggering event, or a
257	  restatement of the user's prompt rather than the underlying question; OR the success criteria
258	  are absent while the Essence Statement itself is present; OR the section uses the honest-depth
259	  escape valve with a reason that is generic and would apply equally to any analysis (e.g.,
260	  "no essence was needed").
261	
262	- **Absent** — no Essence Statement is present (the Problem Essence section is empty, contains
263	  only a restatement of the original prompt with no analytical distillation, or the section
264	  heading appears with nothing below it).
265	  This verdict routes back to Phase 1 to re-frame the Essence Statement — or, when the cause is an input that was never supplied, to re-opening input under the Input Contract — rather than an in-place rewrite of output section 1; the route is bounded by the same rule described under `SKILL.md`'s "Before presenting conclusions" section.

295	  "general assumption," "business constraint," freeform labels); OR multiple rows have empty
296	  Verdict or Verification cells; OR every assumption is labelled Accept with no challenge
297	  attempted and no evidence cited for any verdict.

303	### Criterion 3: Establish Ground Truths
304	
305	Scores the **Ground Truths list** — a numbered list of verified facts with stable GT-IDs,
306	source citations, and a provenance label, with unverified and delegate-reported entries marked
307	with the `GT-N?` suffix — in the Ground Truths section (output section 3).
308	
309	**Provenance check (apply before banding).** A citation being present is not verification. For
310	each unsuffixed ground truth, ask whether the analysis read the asserted figure in the cited
311	source — `read-at-source` — or merely received it from a sub-agent, search result, or summary
312	without opening the citation (`reported-by-delegate`, which requires the `?`). Score against
313	what the analysis did, not against how well-formed the citation looks.
314	
315	- **Rigorous** — every GT-item carries a stable identifier (GT-1, GT-2, etc.) that matches
316	  the identifiers referenced in the Derivation Chains section; every verified GT has a source
317	  citation that is more specific than "common knowledge" or "known fact"; every GT carries a
318	  provenance label; every unverified or delegate-reported GT is marked with the `?` suffix;
319	  the `?`-marked GTs are **enumerated by ID** and that enumeration matches the suffixed entries
320	  in the Ground Truths list when checked against it; every unsuffixed GT feeding a
321	  HIGH-confidence chain names its read-at-source location; no assumption that was discarded in
322	  Phase 2 (Verdict: Discard) appears in this list. Every unsuffixed GT whose cited source is
323	  reachable feeds at least one HIGH-confidence chain EXCEPT: the Phase 3 failure record names
324	  the source as unreachable, in which case the GT may feed only MEDIUM or LOW chains, evidenced
325	  by that record naming which source and why unreachable.
326	
327	  **Check the enumeration, do not quote it.** Quoting the analysis's own provenance summary as
328	  the satisfying span does not discharge this criterion — that verifies a summary was written,
329	  not that it is correct. Read the Ground Truths list, collect the IDs actually carrying `?`,
330	  and compare against the enumeration. Cite the comparison as the satisfying span (*"enumerated
331	  GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14; list carries `?` on exactly those four"*). Where a stated count and
332	  its enumeration disagree, the enumeration governs and the mismatched count is itself a defect.
333	
334	  **Reachability is decided by the Phase 3 record, not re-decided here.** A source is reachable
335	  when the Phase 3 verification step opened it, and unreachable when the Phase 3 failure record
336	  names it with a specific reason; the analyst reads the record and does not re-argue
337	  reachability per ground truth. This requirement is not satisfied by a ground truth that feeds
338	  no chain at all — a GT no derivation chain consumes is already a Criterion 4 defect, and the
339	  requirement presupposes at least one load-bearing chain consumes the GT. A single unsuffixed
340	  GT whose reachable source feeds only MEDIUM or LOW chains bands this criterion Sound; the same
341	  shortfall across multiple GTs bands it Hand-wavy.
342	
343	- **Sound** — GT-IDs are present and stable, but one or more verified GTs cite "common
344	  knowledge," "known fact," or no source at all; OR provenance labels are missing though the
345	  `?` suffixes themselves are correctly applied; OR one unread GT (unverified or
346	  delegate-reported) is used without the `?` suffix **and it feeds only MEDIUM or LOW
347	  confidence chains**; OR the `?`-marked GTs are summarized by a bare count rather than
348	  enumerated, though the suffixes in the list are themselves correct.
349	
350	  An enumeration that **disagrees with the list** does not band here — it bands **Hand-wavy**.
351	  A count that merely accompanies a correct enumeration and disagrees with it is a defect but
352	  bands Sound, since the enumeration governs and remains checkable.
353	
354	- **Hand-wavy** — GT-IDs are present but they are not stable (the same ID is used for
355	  different facts at different points in the document, or IDs are renumbered between sections);
356	  OR the list includes an assumption that was assigned a Discard verdict in Phase 2; OR
357	  multiple unread GTs are used in chains without the `?` suffix; OR **the `?` enumeration
358	  disagrees with the Ground Truths list** — an enumeration that omits a suffixed GT understates
359	  the analysis's unverified inputs in the direction that flatters it, and unlike a bare count it
360	  was checkable, so a mismatch is a stronger failure than never enumerating at all; OR **any
361	  unsuffixed GT feeds a HIGH-confidence chain without naming a read-at-source location** — a
362	  HIGH-confidence conclusion resting on a figure nobody read is the failure this criterion
363	  exists to catch, and a single instance is enough to land here.
364	
365	  **Fix — acquire before you downgrade.** Branch one, preferred: acquire the evidence — open
366	  the cited source, per the Phase 3 verification step, and let the read move the provenance
367	  label. Branch two: downgrade the confidence — carry the `?` and drop the chain from HIGH,
368	  taken only when the source cannot be opened or opens without containing the asserted figure or wording. The preference, explicitly: acquisition is preferred when the source is reachable, because a gate whose only available Fix weakens the output resolves every failure toward less claim rather than more evidence. The unreachable case is not a free pass — the downgrade branch still requires the Phase 3 failure record, which source and why unreachable, or `citation does not support the claim`, so a reader can tell a downgrade from a skipped attempt.
369	
370	- **Absent** — no GT-IDs are assigned to any fact in the Ground Truths section; OR the Ground
371	  Truths section lists claims without distinguishing verified from unverified (no `?` suffix
372	  appears anywhere, no citations appear anywhere, and the list is undifferentiated); OR the
373	  section is absent or empty.

375	### Criterion 4: Reason Upward
376	
377	Scores **both** the **Derivation Chains** (output section 4) — one chain per conclusion,
378	formatted as `GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]` with at least one
379	intermediate step — **and** the **Abandoned Reasoning** section (output section 5).
380	Both sections are in scope for this criterion. Quoted span: where the band is determined by chain form or chain dependency, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's chain-form table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Derivation Chains prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Abandoned Reasoning section, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban, a missing `[Assumes: X]` declaration, or hop validity and arithmetic — none of which the chain-form table carries a column for — quote the analysis text directly. Folds in:
381	dead-end honesty, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban (D-07), escape-valve policing for Abandoned
382	Reasoning (D-03), and hop validity and arithmetic. The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
383	
384	- **Rigorous** — every conclusion stated anywhere in the document (in section 4 or section 6)
385	  has exactly one derivation chain in section 4; each chain names the inputs it consumes — ground truths, upstream conclusions, or both — in the prescribed head form (`GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])`),
386	  contains at least one intermediate claim (a claim that cannot be stated from any single named input alone), and reaches a conclusion; each chain is rendered in the prescribed
387	  arrow-led form. A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples. Hops rendered as an ordered list do not satisfy the prescribed form; the Abandoned Reasoning
388	  section either documents

## Adversarial pass (process output)

**Recompute.** GT-6? bracket: lower scenario 1,200 DAU × 20 req/user/day × 15% peak-hour
concentration × 5× intra-hour burst ÷ 3,600 s = 5.0 req/s. Upper scenario 1,200 × 200 × 25% ×
8× ÷ 3,600 = 133.3 req/s. Both recomputed independently and match the figures used in chain C1.
GT-7? bracket: low end 4 additional services × 10 hrs/month = 40 hrs ÷ 960 team-hours/month
(6 engineers × 160 hrs) = 4.2%; high end 5 additional services × 20 hrs/month = 100 hrs ÷ 960 =
10.4%. Both recomputed and match the figures used in chains C4 and C6. Trade-off weighted totals
(chain C6) recomputed from the six scored criteria: A = 92, B = 93, C = 68 — matches. Flip test
recomputed: reducing criterion 5's weight from 3 to 2 changes the totals to A = 90, B = 88 —
confirmed as the minimal single-weight flip (Δ = 1, the smallest possible move on the 1–5 scale).

**Sensitivity.** The single ground truth whose falsity would most flip the headline conclusion is
GT-6? (it is `?`-marked): if this team's actual traffic shape is far more concentrated or far
chattier than the bracketed range (e.g., heavy background/batch load, or a client polling far
more aggressively than modeled), the "no scaling problem exists" premise under C1 weakens, and
C4/C6 weaken with it. Verification path: instrument real production APM data for one review cycle
and recompute against measured req/s instead of assumed unit-factors (named as a Falsification
condition below). Weakest link per chain: C1 → GT-6?'s assumed traffic-shape factors; C3 → A11
(priced; endpoint still stands on GT-1 alone if A11 fails, so this is not the chain's true
weakest point, listed for completeness); C4 and C6 → GT-7?'s assumed per-service overhead-hour
estimate.

**Rival.** Headline conclusion: the strongest rival is "adopt microservices now via the Inverse
Conway Maneuver, to pre-shape a future multi-team org" — ruled out in §5, Dead End 1 (GT-7?'s
near-certain recurring cost outweighs a speculative future benefit with no stated near-term
org-growth plan). C1: rival is "growth could be materially faster than modeled" — settled inline
on C1's own confidence line (even the pessimistic 133 req/s end of the bracket remains trivial
against single-deployable throughput). C2 and C3: same Inverse-Conway rival as the headline
conclusion, ruled out by the same §5 entry. C4 and C6: rival is "the Prime Video case (GT-5?) is a
narrow billing/orchestration-specific outlier (AWS Step Functions per-state-transition billing),
not a general indictment of microservices" — this rival is not fully dismissed, but C4's
conclusion is independently supported by GT-1 (Fowler's general premium principle) and GT-7?
(this team's own Fermi-derived cost estimate), neither of which depends on the Prime Video case,
so the conclusion is unaffected even granting the rival reading in full. C5: rival is "these
second-order effects are speculative and may not materialize" — not separately settled; this is
already priced into C5's MEDIUM band (capped by citing C4, and A14/A15 both carry the
`unverified — flagged` notation).

**Premise.** It is now eighteen months later. The team invested in a modular monolith rather than
adopting microservices, and that decision has turned out to be a failure — the product suffered
materially as a result.

**Causes.** (Generated unfiltered, before grouping, from four viewpoints: the engineers
implementing the plan, the customers living with its results, the founder/eng-lead paying for it,
and a competitor who benefits from the team's missteps.)
1. (engineer) The "modular monolith" discipline was never mechanically enforced, so the codebase
   decayed back into a tangled monolith within two quarters, invalidating the trade-off's
   "cheap future extraction" score.
2. (engineer) A single bad deploy or memory leak in one module took the entire product down
   during a critical business moment, because nothing separated failure domains.
3. (engineer) DAU grew far faster than GT-6?'s bracket modeled (a viral feature, a major
   enterprise win), and the monolith hit a real scaling ceiling before the team could react.
4. (engineer) One specific workload turned out to have a genuinely different resource profile
   from the rest of the app (e.g., a compute-heavy feature), and being stuck in one deployable
   made it impossible to scale that piece without over-provisioning everything else.
5. (customer) Feature delivery slowed as the monolith became a "big ball of mud" under six
   engineers with no enforced boundaries, and customers churned to a faster-moving competitor.
6. (founder/eng-lead) Hiring suffered: candidates seeking "modern" distributed-systems experience
   passed on the role, hampering hiring for a specific growth phase.
7. (founder/eng-lead) When the org later split from 6 to 20 engineers across two product lines,
   the un-decomposed monolith made that split expensive and slow — the named flip condition was
   noticed too late, because nothing was actively watching for it.
8. (competitor) A well-funded rival who over-invested in microservices early happened to scale
   unusually fast, and it paid off for them specifically — an outlier this analysis's central
   estimate does not weight heavily but which nonetheless occurred.

**Clusters.**
- **Cluster A — Discipline decay** (causes 1). Bears on: C6, and the trade-off's criterion 5
  (future-extraction optionality) and criterion 2 (ops-fit), whose scores assume the modular
  boundaries are actually maintained.
- **Cluster B — Fault-isolation exposure** (cause 2). Bears on: C6's fault-isolation criterion
  (scored 2–3 of 5 for the monolith/modular-monolith options).
- **Cluster C — Growth-rate mis-estimate** (causes 3, 4). Bears on: GT-6?, C1, C6.
- **Cluster D — Late flip-condition detection** (cause 7). Bears on: C2, C3, and the Conclusion's
  stated flip conditions.
- **Cluster E — Heterogeneous-workload blind spot** (cause 4, restated as a structural gap rather
  than an event). Bears on: GT-6?, C1.
- Causes 5, 6, 8 are downstream restatements of Clusters A/C rather than independent structural
  weaknesses (slower delivery, weaker hiring, and a competitor's success are consequences of
  discipline decay and growth mis-estimate, not separate root causes) and are folded into those
  clusters' dispositions rather than given their own.

**Disposition.**
- Cluster A — plan change: modular-monolith boundaries must be mechanically enforced (dependency-
  direction lint rules, module-level CODEOWNERS, a recurring architecture review), not merely
  declared, converting C6's assumption into an enforced practice.
- Cluster B — accepted risk, named mitigation: accept single-process fault-isolation exposure for
  now; mitigate the highest-risk paths (e.g., background jobs, anything prone to resource
  exhaustion) with separate worker/queue processes short of a full service split.
- Cluster C — plan change: instrument real production traffic now and set the Falsification
  condition below as an active tripwire rather than relying on the one-time Fermi bracket
  indefinitely.
- Cluster D — plan change: name an explicit owner and a quarterly checkpoint that re-evaluates the
  three flip conditions (headcount, load, org structure) against current data.
- Cluster E — accepted risk, named mitigation: if a workload with a genuinely different resource
  profile is added, that specific workload becomes an immediate extraction candidate on its own
  merits, independent of the rest of this recommendation — Cluster A's enforced boundaries are
  what make that single extraction cheap when it happens.

**Falsification.** This conclusion is false if, within the next two quarterly review cycles, the
team measures real production peak load exceeding roughly 1,000–2,000 sustained req/s on the
current single-deployable setup with no easy horizontal-scaling headroom left; or the org grows
past roughly 10–12 engineers organized into genuinely separate sub-teams each owning a distinct
business capability; or a single workload emerges with a resource profile (e.g., GPU/ML-bound)
that cannot reasonably be co-scaled with the rest of the monolith. Any one of these observations
flips the recommendation toward extracting at least that piece as an independent service.

# First-Principles Analysis: Should a 6-Engineer Team at ~1,200 DAU Adopt Microservices?

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Given a six-engineer team running one monolithic deployable at roughly 1,200
daily active users, does the actual (not analogized) cost/benefit balance of splitting into
microservices favor adopting microservices now, or does it favor a different architecture
investment — and at what team-size, load, or workload-shape thresholds does that balance flip?

**Success criteria:**
1. The recommendation is derived from ground truths about what microservices structurally buy
   (independent scaling, fault isolation, team-boundary alignment) and what they cost (recurring
   operational tax, cross-service coordination overhead), not from analogy to companies at a
   different scale.
2. The analysis states specific team-size and load thresholds at which the trade-off flips,
   sourced from evidence, not intuition.
3. The "FAANG does it, so we should too" argument is explicitly tested and either upheld or
   discharged with a first-principles or evidenced counter.
4. The analysis ends in one clear recommendation with named flip conditions that let the team
   re-decide later without redoing the whole analysis.

---

## 2. Assumptions Table

|---|---|---|---|---|

| Microservices are inherently "good engineering practice" / more professional | convention | Explicitly challenge before use | Challenge — value is context-dependent per GT-1, not a universal good | GT-1 |
| If FAANG uses microservices, this team should too | convention | Explicitly challenge before use | Discard — reasoning by analogy; GT-3 and GT-5? show organizational scale and Amazon's own internal experience cut the other way | GT-3, GT-5? (unverified — flagged) |

| A monolith cannot be deployed independently or continuously | convention | Explicitly challenge before use | Discard — CI/CD, feature flags, and trunk-based development work on a monolith; deployment frequency is decoupled from service count | GT-2 |

**Inversion pass (Phase 2 companion technique).** Claim tested: "adopting microservices now is
the right architecture decision for this team." Inverted: "it fails." Failure-guaranteeing
conditions enumerated: (1) plumbing overhead drops feature velocity for multiple quarters; (2) no
current or near-term load/fault-isolation problem exists that decomposition actually solves; (3)
the team lacks dedicated platform/SRE capacity, so the tax falls on the same six people who would
otherwise ship product; (4) service boundaries are drawn wrong before real usage data reveals the
actual seams, forcing costly re-decomposition; (5) on-call burden rises disproportionately for a
six-person rotation with no dedicated ops role; (6) new hires ramp more slowly because
distributed-systems literacy becomes a baseline requirement. Necessary preconditions derived from
these, each stated as a checkable assertion: P1 "the team has spare capacity to absorb the
recurring tax without slowing delivery" (load-bearing: yes; status: FALSE per GT-7? and A9 — no
dedicated ops role exists); P2 "a genuine scaling or fault-isolation problem exists today that
only decomposition can solve" (load-bearing: yes; status: FALSE per GT-6?/C1); P3 "service
boundaries can be drawn correctly on the first attempt without real production usage data"
(load-bearing: yes; status: untested belief, folded into the existing "splitting now avoids a
costly rewrite later" row above); P4 and P5 (load-bearing: no; situational) become A12 and A13
above. Two of the three load-bearing preconditions (P1, P2) are currently false, and the third
(P3) is an unverified belief the industry consensus leans against — this is what drives the
inversion's finding into the Assumptions Table rather than the reverse.

## 3. Ground Truths

- **GT-1** Martin Fowler's Microservice Premium: microservices impose a productivity cost repaid
  only by managing genuine complexity; "don't even consider microservices unless you have a
  system that's too complex to manage as a monolith." — source: Martin Fowler, "MicroservicePremium,"
  https://martinfowler.com/bliki/MicroservicePremium.html; read-at-source: the article's
  central-claim paragraphs, quoted directly and confirmed present on the page.
- **GT-2** Fowler on modularity and team size: modularity's importance grows with team size, but
  the article states no explicit numeric team-size or service-count threshold — architectural
  guidance is contextual, not formulaic. — source: Martin Fowler, "Microservice Trade-Offs,"
  https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservice-trade-offs.html; read-at-source: the team-size
  and Microservice Premium paragraphs, quoted directly and confirmed present on the page.
- **GT-3** Conway's original 1968 thesis: "Any organization that designs a system ... will produce
  a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure." — source:
  Melvin Conway, "Conway's Law" (reproducing the 1968 Datamation paper),
  https://www.melconway.com/Home/Conways_Law.html; read-at-source: the thesis-statement paragraph,
  quoted verbatim and confirmed present on the page.
- **GT-4** Amazon's "two-pizza team" heuristic caps a single cohesive team-unit at roughly under
  10 people, justified by reduced communication lines/bureaucracy and by countering the
  Ringelmann effect (the documented tendency for individual productivity and accountability to
  decline as group size grows). — source: AWS Executive Insights, "Amazon's Two-Pizza Teams,"
  https://aws.amazon.com/executive-insights/content/amazon-two-pizza-team/; read-at-source: the
  team-size and Ringelmann-effect paragraphs, quoted directly and confirmed present on the page.
- **GT-5?** Amazon's own Prime Video audio/video monitoring team replaced a distributed
  serverless/microservices design with a monolith after the original design "hit a hard scaling
  limit at around 5% of the expected load," and the change "saved them a staggering 90% on
  operating costs, and simplified the system too." — cited to: Amazon's Prime Video Tech Blog,
